items: Only lists, ranges and containers survive a second `for`.
Generators and genexps do not.
Rule 1: iterate twice, index, or sort → materialize a list.

blocks.title: The Cheap Test
blocks.text: Ask whether the data is walked once. If yes, stay lazy. If no, pay the O(n) memory and take the list.

items: Rule 2: unbounded, huge, or I/O-streamed → generator.
Rule 3a: one expression → genexp.
Rule 3b: branching, state, cleanup → generator function.
Rule 3c: rich domain object → iterator class.
Rule 4: the operation already has an itertools name.
chain, islice, groupby, accumulate — use it, don't hand-roll.
Iterable → has `__iter__`.
Iterator → has `__iter__` and `__next__`.
Generator → an iterator the compiler wrote for you.
`for` = `iter()` + repeated `next()` + `StopIteration`.
`yield` freezes a frame; `next()` thaws it.
`return` closes it, value lands in `StopIteration.value`.
`send`/`throw`/`close` = two-way coroutine.
`yield from` forwards all three to a subgenerator.

blocks.text: Memory O(1) vs O(n) is the headline win. Per-item frame overhead is the price you pay for it.

items: Reusing an exhausted generator.
Late-binding closures over the loop variable.
PEP 479 `StopIteration` leakage out of a generator body.
Reach for itertools before writing a loop.
islice, chain, groupby, accumulate, tee, batched.
Stack genexps for constant-memory ETL over files.
Same pattern works over unbounded network streams.

blocks.title: Default Setting
blocks.text: Lazy for I/O and large data. Eager for small data reused more than once. Everything else is a measurement, not an opinion.

caption.text: Part 2 of ITERATORS & GENERATORS. Most Python devs write `yield` for years without ever seeing what it actually does: it freezes a stack frame on the heap and hands the caller a bookmark. This handbook walks the whole iteration model — iter/next mechanics, hand-rolled iterator classes, generator internals (gi_frame, GeneratorExit, PEP 479), lazy pipelines, itertools, and the silent-zero bugs that only show up in production. Save it for the next time `sum(g)` returns 0 and nothing raises.
